To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the species richness of fossil and recent mammal communities are positively related, that the relationship between fossil and recent species richness is not a simple one, that the fossil species richness of a community is not simply related to the species richness of the modern community that replaced it, that the species richnesses of modern mammal communities are significantly related to their geographic areas, and that the species richness and geographic areas of fossil and modern communities can be predicted from each other.
the species richness of the fossil mammal fauna of the Eocene and Oligocene of the northern Rocky Mountain region is 2.5 times that of the extant mammal fauna of this region.
The fossil record of mammals is compatible with an evolutionary tree model, but it also contains features that are difficult to reconcile with the model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the evolution of the mammalian skull and its relationship to the evolution of the jaw, teeth, and the brain.
understanding the evolution and ecology of species, and the role of species in the structure and dynamics of ecological communities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fossil mammalian fauna is a very close and faithful representation of the fauna of today.

, as a rule, species are not found to be limited by definite boundaries, but that they are found to be limited in range by a number of factors, including climate and other physical conditions, food supply, competition, and other conditions of life, and that these factors are not always the same in all cases, but vary with the species.
the range of variation in any species is very great, but the limits of the species are definite.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the species and subspecies are not the units of nature, but are the products of our minds, based upon our observations of nature, which we have found to be the most useful way of classifying the living things of our world.
the species of mammals are not fixed and unchanging, but are subject to considerable variation.

the fossil mammal faunas of the world are not only of great interest in the history of the earth’s surface and climate, but that they are of the greatest value in the study of the evolution of mammal species.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can’t just look at the species that are present in a fossil assemblage to infer what the climate was like.
the fossil record does not support a simple model in which a species is defined by its morphology and its niche, and then persists unchanged for millions of years.
we should not expect to find a single species in any given fossil site, but instead a range of species that reflect the changing climate and habitat over time.
